summary: Skamania County summit: 1942 L-4 tower on a disputed 1930 cab, 1942-43 aircraft warning post, removed 1967; garage base and barriers remain.

facts.design: 10-foot wooden tower with an L-4 cab (1942); a 15-foot wooden live-in cab is listed for 1930 but disputed
facts.status_note: Lookout removed or destroyed in 1967; a garage foundation and concrete parking barriers are reported at the site
facts.agency: Washington Division of Forestry/U.S. Forest Service

access.note: The official route is the Pacific Crest Trail from the Bonneville Trailhead. The older road route crosses posted private land, and Willhite reports a trespass threat there.

visit.trail_note: PCT from the Bonneville Trailhead in North Bonneville, 11 miles out and back (Willhite). Willhite lists hiking or 4WD/high-clearance access; the drive route crosses posted private land.

events.note: First lookout listed as a 15-foot wooden live-in cab. Willhite doubts this, citing a 1938 survey with no building.
Road built to the summit; a 10-foot wooden tower with an L-4 cab went up
Aircraft Warning Service used the lookout from October 7, 1942 to October 16, 1943. Willhite says a garage was built with AWS funds.
Registered June 20, 2012 as US 1305, WA 205; nominated by Ray Kresek

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The lookout inventory, as cited by FFLOS and firelookout.com, dates a 15-foot live-in cab to 1930. Willhite doubts it, citing a 1938 survey with no building, and dates the first sure lookout to 1942. The story gives both.
FFLOS gives 1,141 ft (348 m) and Willhite gives a summit of 1,129 ft. The brief's 347.8 m is kept.

sources.title: Aldrich Butte Fire Lookout - North Bonneville WA

notes_for_editor: Four sources agree on the 1942 tower, the 1946 cabin, the 1942-43 Aircraft Warning Service dates and the 1967 removal. The 1930 cab is disputed: the inventory gives it, Willhite doubts it. No lookout is named for any period, so staffing is left out of facts. Today's state rests on Willhite's and the FFLOS photo captions, which are undated. The drive route is described only as crossing posted private land; the story steers readers to the trail. Brief record matches all four sources on status and registration. Read budget: 4 page reads (FFLOS, firelookout.com, Willhite, Weebly) plus the firelookout.org index used for three records.
